digest.top_line: TORPEdO: IMPT vs IMRT chemoRT in locally advanced OPSCC, 12-mo tube dependence/severe weight loss 18% vs 7% (p=0.079), UW-QoL 78.3 vs 77.1 (p=0.56), no functional gain.
digest.tldr: The one head-neck readout: TORPEdO, a phase 3 RCT of IMPT vs IMRT (N=205, 70 Gy/33 fx + cisplatin). Protons lowered OAR doses but gave no 12-mo functional gain. Tube dependence/severe weight loss was 18% vs 7% (p=0.079) and UW-QoL 78.3 vs 77.1 (p=0.56). Weigh this against missed fractions in 49% of IMPT pts and a two-centre pathway confound.

sites.intro: TORPEdO is the randomised test of whether IMPT's OAR dose sparing buys a functional benefit in chemoRT for OPSCC, and at 12 mo it did not.

studies.name: TORPEdO
studies.tldr: IMPT vs IMRT in locally advanced OPSCC: 12-mo tube dependence/severe weight loss 18% vs 7% (p=0.079), UW-QoL 78.3 vs 77.1 (p=0.56).
details: 🔍 Phase 3 open-label RCT, 2:1, 20 UK NHS hospitals, N=205 (136 IMPT, 69 IMRT)
🔍 Both arms 70 Gy / 56 Gy in 33 fx over 6.5 wk plus cisplatin 100 mg/m² x2
📊 Co-primary and exploratory endpoints, IMPT vs IMRT

⚠️ IMPT missed fractions in 65 (49%) of 132 pts, cyclotron breakdown in 47 (72%) of 65
⚠️ Unmasked; IMPT at 2 national centres vs IMRT at local referring centre, pathway confound
⚠️ UW-QoL co-primary evaluable in only 154 (75%) of 205

verdict.rationale: Randomised phase 3 with both prespecified co-primaries null, against the dosimetric and NTCP rationale for IMPT. Open-label design does not undermine a null result.
verdict.audience: Locally advanced OPSCC (96% p16+), cisplatin CRT, N3 excluded

studies.monday_clinic: In cisplatin-eligible locally advanced OPSCC (96% p16-positive) receiving 70 Gy bilateral neck CRT, this does not support IMPT referral for an expected 12-mo swallowing or QoL gain over IMRT; it does not extend to N3 disease, induction chemotherapy or upfront neck dissection.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase 3, multicentre, open-label RCT** at 20 UK NHS hospitals, randomised **2:1** by minimisation, N=205 (136 IMPT, 69 IMRT), Feb 2020 to June 2023. Median follow-up **28.3 mo** (IQR 26.5 to 39.3).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Newly diagnosed **locally advanced oropharyngeal SCC** suitable for concurrent CRT including bilateral neck treatment; **96% p16-positive**. 99 (48%) T3 or T4 and 44 (22%) bilateral nodal involvement; excluded N3, upfront neck dissection, induction chemotherapy and pre-treatment feeding tube.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Two cycles **high-dose cisplatin 100 mg/m²** every 3 weeks. 138 (69%) of 199 received both cisplatin cycles and 49 (25%) received cisplatin then carboplatin.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Both arms **70 Gy** to therapeutic target and **56 Gy** to lower-risk volumes in **33 daily fractions over 6.5 weeks**, RBE 1.1 for IMPT, with standardised outlining, planning priorities and replanning criteria. IMPT typically used five beams, with plans evaluated against 3-mm setup error and 3.5% range uncertainty. Replanning was needed in **81 (61%) of 132** IMPT vs **20 (30%) of 67** IMRT pts.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Co-primary at 12 mo:** gastrostomy-tube dependence or severe weight loss (≥20% from baseline), and UW-QoL mean physical composite score, α=0.025 each with either sufficient for success. Loco-regional recurrence and OS were **exploratory**, tested at 1%.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Neither co-primary met**; the clinical composite was driven by weight loss, not tube dependence. Prespecified and post-hoc sensitivity analyses were consistent with the primary analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: 14 SAEs in 12 pts, **five treatment-related (one IMPT vs four IMRT)**, with **no treatment-related deaths**. Most common SAEs were acute kidney injury and thromboembolism.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Tests the dosimetric premise behind proton referral in OPC: IMPT lowered doses to most OARs without a 12-mo functional gain. The Dutch NTCP thresholds did not isolate a benefiting group, with overlapping enriched-cohort UW-QoL intervals. Read alongside the MD Anderson randomised IMPT vs IMRT trial in the same disease.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents cisplatin-eligible locally advanced OPSCC, predominantly p16-positive, treated with 70 Gy/33 fx CRT including bilateral neck. Does not represent N3 disease, induction chemotherapy, upfront neck dissection, or pts needing a feeding tube before treatment.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: 2:1 allocation left **69 IMRT pts**, so intervals are wide and disease-control endpoints uninformative. IMPT was centralised at two centres with cyclotron-driven interruptions, confounding modality with care pathway, and UW-QoL was evaluable in **154 (75%) of 205**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors conclude **IMRT remains standard of care** where IMPT is not routine. The IMPT weight-loss excess persisted to 24 mo; whether it reflects the modality, delivery interruptions, or nutritional follow-up at distant referral centres is unsettled.

studies.interpretation:
The case for protons in oropharyngeal cancer has rested on a dosimetric chain: lower dose to swallowing structures, oral cavity and salivary glands, translated through NTCP models into predicted reductions in dysphagia, xerostomia and tube dependence, and in some systems used directly as a referral threshold. TORPEdO is a randomised test of whether that chain holds at 12 months in cisplatin-treated locally advanced disease, and in this population it did not. IMPT delivered lower doses to most organs at risk, including the highest-priority structures, yet the patient-reported physical composite was essentially flat between arms (difference 1.3, 97.5% CI -3.7 to 6.2) and the clinical composite leaned the other way.

That lean deserves more attention than its p-value. The composite was not driven by tube dependence, which was 2% in both arms, but by grade 3 weight loss, which ran 18% vs 6% at 12 months and 13% vs none at 24 months, having been absent in both arms at the end of chemoradiotherapy. A dose-mediated toxicity should favour IMPT, so a late divergence against it points toward something outside the plan: nutritional follow-up after treatment at a distant national centre, differing tube practice (prophylactic placement was less frequent in the IMPT arm), or body habitus, since the IMPT excess in grade 2 or worse weight loss concentrated in pts with baseline BMI ≥25. Treatment was unmasked and modality is inseparable from care pathway in this design, so the trial cannot attribute the excess to protons themselves; equally, it offers no support for the claim that protons reduce it.

Delivery conditions were those of a new national service rather than a long-established programme. Nearly half of IMPT pts had a missed fraction, mostly from cyclotron breakdown, though compensation held median radiotherapy duration at 44 days in both arms, and replanning was needed in 61% vs 30%. OAR doses did not differ between the first and second halves of accrual, which weakens a learning-curve explanation for the null result.

The trial is not built to speak to disease control. With 69 pts in the IMRT arm, the loco-regional HR of 2.6 carries a 99% CI of 0.3 to 20.3, compatible with anything from meaningful benefit to meaningful harm, and time-to-event endpoints were exploratory. Concern about range uncertainty and target coverage with protons is neither raised nor retired by these data.

What changes is the selection argument. The pre-planned enriched cohort, pts meeting Dutch NTCP thresholds, showed overlapping UW-QoL intervals, though enrichment was unbalanced by arm (62% of 99 IMPT vs 31% of 54 IMRT evaluable pts), which makes that analysis fragile rather than conclusive. For a health system deciding whether to extend IMPT to predominantly p16-positive oropharyngeal cancer on functional grounds, the randomised basis is now absent, and the authors keep IMRT as standard where IMPT is not routine. The read would be wrong if late effects such as jaw osteonecrosis or late dysphagia diverge beyond 24 months, or if the weight-loss signal proves to be a pathway artefact that a co-located proton service would not reproduce. Readers weighing this against the MD Anderson randomised IMPT vs IMRT trial should compare endpoints and delivery setting before treating the two as discordant.
